text: Graham told me to stop running his brother's workshop, so I stopped. Nine days later, inspectors shut the whole place down. I'm 31, a licensed structural engineer, married to Graham for four years. His younger brother Reese opened the custom furniture shop four years ago with a small business loan and no safety training at all. From the very first month, I signed off on everything myself. Shelving loads, mezzanine weight limits, wiring near the finishing booth. Nobody paid me for it. Nobody ever asked me to stop. Then three weeks ago, a client watched me correct one of Reese's rigging diagrams in front of him, and Reese told Graham I made him look incompetent in his own shop. That night, Graham said I needed to let his brother run his own business for once. I didn't argue. I just stopped answering Reese's text. The annual recertification was due that same month, and I let the deadline pass without filing it. Nine days later, the county fire marshal did a routine walkthrough and found no current structural sign-off on file anywhere. He shut the shop down on the spot, pending a full recertification. What Reese never knew was how close that shop had already come to disaster. Two years ago, I found a mezzanine storage loft rated to hold half of what he was stacking on it. Last spring, I caught wiring running six inches from the lacquer booth, close enough to start a fire in seconds. I fixed both quietly and told nobody, not even Graham. Reese had a delivery due for a hotel chain called Bellamy & Finch worth $82,000 due the second week of December, with a penalty clause for every day it was late. Closing the shop was costing him roughly $1,000 a day. He called me 11 times in four days. I didn't answer once. On the fifth day, I drove over to return a mixer I'd borrowed, not to check on him. Sitting open on his desk was the county's recertification binder. A new structural sign-off page was already filed inside it, dated two days after our fight, carrying my license number and a signature that was not mine. I called the inspector's office listed on the form. She confirmed it had been accepted and to reopen that same morning. I asked Graham if he'd known. He said, Reese wouldn't do that. He did, I said. Graham stared at the binder, then asked, You've been signing off on that place since the beginning? Yes, I said. Why would he forge it instead of just calling you? Because he knew I'd say no. A forged engineering stamp is not a family disagreement. It is a felony filed under my license number, not his. I called the county that afternoon and reported the signature myself, before an inspector or an insurance auditor found at first. The shop closed again within the hour, this time flagged for fraud instead of a routine violation. Reese has not called since that day. Graham sleeps on his own side of the bed again, not the couch, but he has not brought up the workshop since either.
